name: Star apple
summary: How Filipino growers raise kaimito, the purple or green star apple of the cool months, from a seedling or a marcot to the first fruit. It is a big, slow, long lived backyard and orchard tree, so the guide is about good spacing, a low shape and careful picking.
season: Trees are planted as the rains begin, about May to July. Kaimito flowers in the rainy months and the fruit ripens about four to five months later, from about late December to March or April.
material: Many backyard trees grow from seeds of a big, sweet fruit. The seeds sprout in two to six weeks and the tree bears in five to six years or more. Growers who want early, true to type fruit plant marcotted or cleft grafted seedlings, grafted onto kaimito seedlings six to eight months old, bought from a nursery or made from their best tree.
spacing: About 10 to 12 m between trees each way, since kaimito grows wide. One seedling or marcot a hole. In backyards, one tree well away from the house.
water: Rain fed. Young trees get water once or twice a week in long dry spells. Old trees stand drought but bear better with water in very dry years.
fertilizer: Compost and rotted manure at planting. Young trees get small amounts of ammonium sulfate (21 0 0) twice a year. Bearing trees get complete fertilizer (14 14 14), about half a kilo twice a year at first and more as the tree grows, at the start and near the end of the rains, spread in a ring under the edge of the leaves.
care: Ring weeding, mulching, watering young trees in dry spells, keeping two or three main branches, removing drooping branches and water sprouts, and bagging young fruit against fruit flies. Birds and bats take ripe fruit, so it is picked often.
harvest: Fruit is ready four to five months after flowering, mostly between late December and March or April. It is picked one by one when fully colored and slightly soft, cut with its stalk, because it does not ripen well once picked. Ripe fruit keeps only a few days at room temperature.

ways.label: Seedlings in bags (punla, binhi o marcot)

steps.title: Sow seeds from ripe fruit
steps.how: Wash the seeds of a big, sweet, fully ripe fruit and sow them about 1 cm deep in a seedbox or bed of loose soil under light shade. Keep the soil damp. They come up in two to six weeks.

steps.title: Marcot a branch of your best tree
steps.how: To get a tree that fruits like your best kaimito, and sooner than a seedling, root a branch while it is still on the tree, then cut it off and raise it in a bag before planting.

parts.title: Pick the tree and the branch
parts.how: Choose a tree that bears good fruit every year, has no pest or disease and is not too old. On it, pick a branch of middle age, about as thick as a finger, pointing upward, out in the sun and without flowers or fruit.

parts.title: Mix the wrapping soil
parts.how: Mix moist garden soil with rice hull, or use the mudpress from a sugar mill. It should hold together in the hand without dripping.

parts.title: Peel a ring of bark
parts.how: With a clean, sharp knife, cut twice around the branch a short distance apart and peel off the bark between the cuts. Scrape away the slippery green layer under it, or the bark grows back over the wound instead of making roots.

parts.title: Wrap and tie it
parts.how: Wrap a sheet of plastic around the ring, pack it with a ball of the moist soil mix, and tie both ends tight with plastic straw so the ball cannot slip or dry out.

parts.title: Wait for the roots
parts.how: Leave it on the tree until white roots show plainly through the plastic. Kaimito marcots take about four to seven months to root.
parts.tip: Some growers cut the branch halfway through first and finish the cut about two weeks later, so the new roots get used to living alone.

parts.title: Cut it off and bag it
parts.how: Saw the branch below the root ball, take off the plastic without breaking the ball, and plant it in a 6 by 8 inch bag filled with two parts soil, one part compost and one part rice hull.

parts.title: Nurse it in the shade
parts.how: Keep the new marcot in shade, out of the rain, for two weeks and water it every day. Then move it into the sun, pick off any flowers, and after about four weeks give it a pinch of complete fertilizer.

steps.title: Move seedlings into bags
steps.how: When each seedling has three to five firm leaves, lift it with its soil and set it in a bag of garden soil and compost. Keep the bags in partial shade and water them often.

steps.title: Cleft graft your seedlings
steps.how: Cleft grafting is the most common way kaimito is multiplied here and takes well. A cut shoot from your best tree is joined onto your own kaimito seedlings, so the new trees bear the same fruit and bear sooner.

parts.title: Use seedlings six to eight months old
parts.how: Your bagged kaimito seedlings are ready as rootstock at about six to eight months, when the stem is firm and as thick as the shoots you will graft on.

parts.title: Cut scions from your best tree
parts.how: Early in the morning, cut healthy shoot tips from a tree that bears heavily and has good fruit. Pull off their leaves without hurting the buds, keep them out of the sun so they do not dry, and graft them the same day.

parts.title: Top and split the rootstock
parts.how: Cut off the seedling top where the stem is still growing actively, then split the stump straight down the middle about 2 to 3 cm with a sharp knife.

parts.title: Shape the wedge and fit it
parts.how: Slice the base of the scion into a short wedge on two sides with smooth, clean cuts. Push it into the split so the bark of the scion lines up with the bark of the stock on at least one side.

parts.title: Tie and cover the graft
parts.how: Bind the joint and the whole scion firmly with a strip of thin plastic, then slip a small plastic bag or ice candy wrapper over the top to keep water out. A good tie lets you lift the whole seedling by the scion without moving the joint.

parts.title: Care for the new graft
parts.how: Keep the plants in light shade and rub off every shoot that grows below the joint. When new leaves push out of the scion, remove the cover and unwind the plastic strip, and move the plant to a bigger bag if it outgrows the first.

steps.title: Dig holes with plenty of room
steps.how: Kaimito becomes a wide tree, so dig holes about 50 cm wide and deep about 10 to 12 m apart. Mix the topsoil with rotted manure or compost and put it back.

steps.title: Harden the seedlings
steps.how: A month before planting, move the bags into more sun and water a little less.

steps.title: Plant at the start of the rains
steps.how: On a cloudy day, cut off the bag, set the seedling or marcot at the same depth it grew, firm the soil, water and tie it to a stake.
steps.tip: Keep a grafted seedling's graft joint above the soil.

steps.title: Mulch the base
steps.how: Lay dry grass or leaves around the young tree, a hand's width from the stem, to keep the soil damp and the weeds down.

steps.title: Feed the young tree
steps.how: Scatter a small amount of ammonium sulfate (21 0 0), about 150 to 200 g a tree, in a ring away from the stem, at the start and near the end of the rains. Compost or manure also works.

steps.title: Ring weed and water in dry spells
steps.how: Keep the ring under the tree clean, and water once or twice a week in long dry spells for the first year or two.

steps.title: Shape two or three main branches
steps.how: Let only two or three strong main branches grow, and cut off drooping, crossing branches and upright water sprouts. A low, open tree is easier to pick.

steps.title: Wrap the young fruit
steps.how: Once the tree fruits, wrap young fruits in paper or net bags to keep fruit flies away, and gather and bury fallen, bored fruit.

steps.title: Pick only fully ripe fruit
steps.how: The first crop comes at about five to six years for seedling trees. Pick only ripe fruit: purple types turn deep purple and green types turn shiny pale green, a little soft. Cut the stalk with clippers or use a bamboo pole with a net.
steps.tip: Kaimito picked unripe stays gummy and puckery. Fruits ripen a few at a time, so pick often.

steps.title: Feed and prune after the season
steps.how: After the last fruit, cut out dead and tangled branches and give complete fertilizer (14 14 14) and manure under the edge of the leaves.

ways.note: Seedling trees usually bear at about five to six years. We count the first harvest at 60 months (1,800 days). Grafted and marcotted trees bear years earlier.

mistakes: Planting trees too close together or to the house.
Picking the fruit before it is ripe, so it stays gummy and sour.
Pulling fruit off without its stalk, so it bruises and leaks latex.
Letting the tree grow tall with many weak branches.
Leaving fallen, fly struck fruit under the tree.
better: Plant grafted or marcotted seedlings of a known sweet type for fruit years sooner.
Test the soil and feed by the result, twice a year.
Keep the tree low with two or three main branches.
Bag young fruit, clean up fallen fruit, and use integrated pest management for fruit flies and twig borers.

watering.traditional: Kaimito here is a rain fed backyard tree: young trees get a pail of water once or twice a week in long dry spells for their first year or two, and old trees are left to the rain. In the provinces with a long, harsh dry season, owners with a well water bearing trees while the fruits fill.
watering.method: A pail or hose into a ring basin around the tree, the usual way in backyards. Water in the cool early morning or late afternoon.
watering.rainfed: Plant as the rains begin and keep the ring mulched. Kaimito thrives in the lowlands, even with a clear dry season: it flowers in the rainy months and fills its fruit as the dry months begin, so most rain fed trees bear well. Where the dry season is harsh, plan a few deep waterings for the months the fruit is filling.
watering.dryseason: Young trees: about once a week for the first six months, then once or twice a week in long dry spells. Bearing trees: a deep soak every week or two while the fruit fills. Water when the tree drops too many leaves or the fruits feel less juicy and start to shrivel.
watering.wet: Kaimito needs soil that drains perfectly. Plant on ground where rain water never stands, or on a low mound on flat land, and keep drains open in the rainy months.

schedule.often: Every day or every other day, keeping the soil damp
schedule.amount: A light sprinkle over the box or bed
schedule.why: Seeds sprout in two to six weeks only in damp soil.

schedule.often: Every day or two in partial shade
schedule.amount: Enough to wet each bag through

schedule.often: A little less often, every 2 to 3 days. Soak the bag the day before planting
schedule.amount: Enough to keep the leaves firm
schedule.why: Tougher leaves stand the field sun.

schedule.often: About once a week, more often in hot, dry weeks
schedule.amount: A good soak of the mulched ring around the stem
schedule.why: A young tree needs steady water for its first half year.

schedule.often: Once or twice a week in long dry spells
schedule.amount: A deep soak of the mulched ring
schedule.why: Water in rainless weeks keeps the tree growing without a break.

schedule.often: Only in long rainless periods. Grafted and marcotted trees reach bearing years sooner
schedule.amount: A deep soak of the ring under the leaves
schedule.why: The roots now reach deep enough for normal dry months.

schedule.stage: Flowering and fruit set (in the rainy months)
schedule.often: Rain usually does it. In a dry break, water about once a week
schedule.amount: A deep soak of the ground under the crown
schedule.why: Water during flowering raises fruit set.

schedule.stage: Fruit growth into the dry months, to harvest (about December to April)
schedule.often: Every week or two once the rains stop, above all in provinces with a harsh dry season
schedule.amount: A deep soak under the crown
schedule.why: The fruits fill as the dry season starts, and drought leaves them dry or shrivelled.

critical: The first six months after planting.
Flowering, when a dry break lowers fruit set.
Fruit filling once the rains stop, in places with a long, harsh dry season.

signs.dry: The tree drops too many leaves, and the fruits come less juicy or shrivel on the branch.
signs.wet: Yellowing leaves and poor growth on soil that stays wet.

better: Give bearing trees a deep soak every week or two from the end of the rains until harvest. The fruits stay juicy and full.
Water young trees weekly for their first six months and keep the ring mulched, so they grow without a break.
